Copper Long-term Outlook 

# Executive summary 

As this year has progressed, we have found it necessary to push demand up slightly as stronger Western economies offset a minor reduction in forecast Chinese metal requirements.  Under the pressures of lacklustre markets, unappealing borrowing conditions and less than favourable arbitrage between the LME and the SHFE, Chinese copper processors have taken much longer to turn to new copper supplies and have instead relied upon stock drawdowns to feed their wire and tube mills.  As we were expecting buyers to call on new copper from April or so, it should come as no surprise to see that we have shaved 70kt or so from our prior Chinese forecast demand for this year, and this now stands at 7.564Mt (we are also mindful of looming power restrictions over the forthcoming summer months).  Meanwhile, better demand thus far in the USA and Asia (excluding China) has pushed our global consumption figure up slightly on our last quarterly report, and this now stands at 20.3Mt _vs._ 20.2Mt, reflecting an improvement over what turned out to be a strong 2010, of 5.4%. 

At the same time, the primary supply side has done somewhat better so far this year than we expected (despite a growing list of disruptions), and we have increased our forecast by 120kt metal from the 19.726Mt shown in our Q1 report to 19.840Mt now.  In light of this, our metal market balance has remained in the -450kt to -500kt deficit range for most of this year, and currently stands at -465kt vs. the -480kt or so that we presented in our Q1 report.  While there is no doubt that such tightness has served to keep copper prices as high as they are, given the poor indicators coming out of China largely since the February holidays, we have not been surprised to see a commensurate lack of interest in the red metal by the investor community for much of this second quarter.  Consequently, LME quotes have trailed our expectations as per the end of the first quarter, and we have reduced our 2011 price forecast from the US$9911/t ($4.50/lb) of end-March to US$9586/t ($4.35/lb) in this report. 

Overall base case mine production capability is forecast to decline by 1% p.a. between 2010 and 2025 with output falling from a peak of ~20Mt in 2015 to ~13.85Mt in 2025.  For this year, demand for mine production will exceed available supply by the considerable margin of c.500kt, but will return to near balance for 2012.  From 2013, the shortfall will grow, amounting to almost 42% of base case mine output by 2020. 

Our smelter production forecast for 2011 now stands at 15.6Mt which is 6.9% higher than was the case in 2010.  Copperin-concentrates contributed an estimated 86% (89% in 2009) of overall smelter out

put last year with the balance derived from scrap and purchased blister.  Average primary smelter capacity utilisation rates increased in 2010 to 80.3% from 79.5% in 2009, and should approach 82.5% this year.  Overall, we expect an additional 4.5Mt/a of smelting capacity to be commissioned between the end of 2010 and 2025. 

The majority of the revisions made to our smelter production capability forecasts are largely reflected in the changes to our refinery output estimates and these can be seen in the main report.  Taking these into account, base case global copper refined production _capability_ is now expected to reach 20.4Mt/a in 2011 (+7%), 22.6Mt/a in 2012 (+11%) and 24.4Mt/a in 2013 (+8%).  However, growth is forecast to slow markedly from 2014 onwards with refined production capability expected to decline from 2016 onwards.  As a consequence, overall global capability will increase by only 1.3% p.a. between 2010 and 2025.  In tonnage terms this equates to an increase of ~4.1Mt to 23.1Mt in 2025. 

Our 2012 price profile has firmed up a little since our last report, with the 50kt surplus previously anticipated being overturned to a marginal deficit.  In itself, the change is minor in a 20Mt/a market.  However, when compounded to the revisions to the market in 2013 – in which we have reduced supply and increased demand projections (mainly on the back of higher projected Chinese economic growth rates) to leave a 335kt surplus instead of the prior c.840kt surplus – we believe the risk to prices will remain on the upside for longer than we did only a few months ago prior to the Chinese growth upgrade.  Consequently, we now expect prices in 2012 to average closer to US$9150/t ($4.15/lb) in 2010$ terms, and 2013’s forecast average to approach the $3.30/lb mark at c.US$7275/t.  With large supply-side increases now virtually inevitable, for the three years starting 2014-2016, we expect to see an annual surplus in the market of c.625kt, pushing metal stocks days of consumption levels back up towards 70 days and leaving us with a fundamentally-based annual price forecast for 2016 of US$4400/t ($2.00/lb) in 2010$ terms.  We expect prices to push through the three-dollar level on a consistent basis only well into 2018 as metal stock days of consumption once again return to levels closer to between 50-55 days. 

Any extended period of low copper prices will serve to discourage companies to develop new mines or expand existing operations.  This projected period of low prices between 2015-2018 will result in a turnaround in the market’s fortunes between 2019 and 2020.  During these years prices are expected to rise sharply, reaching a cycle high of $6283-6615/t ($2.85-3.00/lb) in constant 2010$ through the period to 2025. 

Our long-term incentive price remains unchanged at $2.50/lb in current dollars over the period to 2025.  This has been derived from our analysis of mine project incentive prices and projected demand for mine production over this perio

d, although we have made no allowance for potential mining-specific inflation which could further increase this forecast. Metals Market Service Long Term Outlook - June 2011 Page 4 of 33 Copper Long-term Outlook # Demand analysis ## Overview **Demand maintains first quarter pace** Global demand has maintained its solid pace from the first quarter of the year to confirm our relatively upbeat view of consumption. In fact, we now expect a modestly higher outturn for 2011 than we did a quarter ago, with an increase of 5.4% now estimated, compared to 5% previously. However, the overall higher growth masks some downgrades, with China in particular toned down to only 5% growth from 6% in the last _Long Term Outlook_ . Elsewhere, we have upgrade our view of European consumption, although this is largely as a result of raised estimates in Russia, while we have also lifted our growth rate for the United States. As a result, we now expect global refined copper demand to rise by 5.4% this year to 20.3Mt, with annual average growth out to 2025 of 3.5% forecast. **Move to trend forecasting over the long term** This update will be the first to forecast demand and prices using Wood Mackenzie’s own long term “trend” macroeconomic forecasts, deviating from the “cycle” forecast which we have traditionally used. This means that we will strip out the negative economic event that we were previously forecasting for 2019 to give a smoother trend. Significantly, this will make no difference to long term average industrial production growth. At the same time, semis output is improving and with softening in the copper price since February, and in particular, in May, fabricators have even bee

n able to modestly restock from bare bones inventory levels.  However, while all these factors point to improving cathode demand in the short term, firms continue to find it difficult to obtain financing, with yet another increase in banks reserve requirements in June only going to make this situation worse.  Meanwhile, despite moderating industrial production, inflation remains stubbornly high.  As such, although there are plenty of reasons to be bullish on Chinese demand, it must be noted that there are a few to sate the desires of bears as well. 

**Higher premia underscore increased appetite for copper** When premia shot up in March from basement levels the previous month, the catalyst was not improving domestic demand but Japanese producers and traders seeking to meet delivery requirements following the earthquake and subsequent tsunami.  A drop off in premia followed but in May premia were back up at high levels as demand picked up in line with improving Chinese semis output. 

**Let’s talk about stocks** Another of the first indicators of improving demand was a decline in stocks, both on and off exchange.  There has been much talk since the start of the year on bonded warehouse stocks having reached 700kt or even higher, depending on whose estimate is referenced, but these stocks have declined in both April and May, to stand at around 300kt at the time of writing in mid-to-late June.  At the same time, SHFE stocks have also been in steady decline, more than halving between the end of March and the end of May. 

At the same time, the arbitrage window has opened, with average LME copper prices cheaper than those for the near dated SHFE future over April and May.  This ought to prompt an upturn in imports into China, and although this hasn’t materialised as yet, the June imports figure is expected to reveal an increase after shipments in the first four months of the year fell by 29%.  Although it is the levels of material coming into China that typically draw the headline, exports have had their fair share of the limelight over the past few months as a sluggish start to the year for demand and a negative arbitrage window resulted in material moving out of China and into nearby LME registered warehouses in South Korea, Singapore and Malaysia.  The increase in inventories in these locations slowed sharply in May, however, pointing to a

drop-off in exports from China.  As such, in the months to come, net trade should add to the apparent consumption figure from both sides of the equation and support improving apparent demand. 

**Economic data paint less rosy picture** With plenty of positives discussed above, it is only reasonable to highlight the less positive factors that are unfolding in the Chinese market, with most of these related to the economy.  At the head of worries are latest inflation figures for May, which rather than revealing a slow

ing in the rate of price rises, actually showed an acceleration. Indeed, CPI picked up to 5.5% in May, the fastest pace of growth since 2008. In almost a direct response, authorities yet again increased banks reserve requirement a further 50 basis points in mid-June to 21.5%. At the same time, industrial activity, while slowing, isn’t grinding to a halt, with industrial output up by 13.3% in May, although this marks the slowest rate of growth this year. This can be read two ways: either IP is slowing in response to higher interest rates which should lead to lower inflation and as such no further measures are required or inflation is continuing to surge ahead despite slowing industrial activity and suggesting further tightening measures are indeed required. We are not overly concerned by the slowdown in IP as we expect full year growth to come in at around 13%, implying growth below this level in the second half of the year. Inflation is a worry though and provides downside risk to demand growth. The major concern with higher inflation is that this results in further tightening measures from central bankers. Firms are already finding it difficult to finance stocks as borrowing rates rise, with high copper prices making this doubly difficult, despite the recent modest respite that softer SHFE and LME levels have provided. Moreover, it is typically small companies that find it hardest to access credit when credit is rationed but semis producers are typically small in scale, despite a few notable exceptions in China. As such, higher lending rates disproportionately impact fabricators and add further downside risk to our demand outlook for this year and next. **Producers to power down in summer?** A further cloud on the horizon is the potential for power shortages during the peak summer demand season. If shortages were to materialise and power was to be rationed, then the question is who would be hit, smelters and refineries or semis producers? Were smelters and refineries to bear the brunt of the power cuts then refined demand could be met by imports, although with a lag; however, if semis producers were affected then this would directly impact consumption of copper. ###### **Chinese housing starts, under construction and completions –(%)** 120%

**Construction to face slowdown** On the face of it, the Chinese construction market continues to motor along, with housing starts and construction in process still registering double-digit growth, while government plans for low-cost housing add further upside. However, as we have discussed previously, there is a significant mismatch between housing starts and construction in process relative t

o housing completions. As the chart below illustrates, housing starts have been running ahead of the rate of completions for over a year and a half, a development with a potentially severe impact on future housing starts. The implication is that there is a massive build of uncompleted housing, while we understand that much of this is basically complete but has not been classified as completed for a combination of tax reasons and a desire not to flood the housing market with properties and thus depress prices. Add rising interest rates to this mix and there is a recipe for a sharp decline in starts as demand for housing slows because of financing problems, while construction slows because of the build up of inventory. The rising inventory of unfinished homes must also be a drag on developers facing a squeeze on their financing. To counter this overhang and the slowdown that must surely follow there is the much vaunted 36 million affordable homes that are to be built during the latest five year plan. The extent to which Metals Market Service Long Term Outlook - June 2011 Page 6 of 33 Copper Long-term Outlook this will temper a slowdown in broad construction is unclear, particularly as we understand that some of the construction in process will simply be reallocated as affordable housing. That said, there will surely be some new building and while we do not expect that this will be sufficient to mitigate a slowdown in construction overall, it should at least soften the blow. **Auto output to pick up in second half** In the automotive market there has also been a sharp slowdown in activity through this year, with production being hit by the aftermath of sales incentives and also from measures to limit congestion in cities such as Beijing. Automotive production fell by 1.6% in April, although it still remains in positive territory for the year-to-date, while we anticipate an upturn in activity towards the year end to result in full year production growth of 10% this year. Further out, we anticipate a gradual slowing in production growth to the mid-single-digit range. Countering the slowdown in demand from production growth will be a gradual increase in more copper-intensive electric cars towards the end of the forecast period. **Balancing act leans downwards overall** Despite the relatively bullish near term developments that we have discussed above, based on data to hand so far this year and expectations of slowing economic and industrial activity in the second half of the year, we have downgraded our full year estimate of refined copper demand this year to 5% growth from 6% previously. However, we expect a rebound in 2012, with demand expanding by 7%. Even so, thus far copper rod production, which accounts for roughly 70% of primary refined copper consumption in the US, has put in a sufficiently strong performance that we expect first half copper demand to be up by 3.8% on H1 2010 at 972kt. Given the strength in demand so far, we expect this year will follow a similar pattern, leaving full year demand at 1.84Mt, or up by 4.6% on 2010. At 110.4kt, rod output was marginally stronger than January’s 109.5kt, and we have to go back to last July to see a higher tonnage than this. Average monthly output this year, at 109kt, has edged out last year’s 105kt, and reflects the stronger automotive market. **Housing market still issuing erratic data** Meanwhile, even t

he housing market has shown signs of bottoming out in some aspects.  May housing starts were up by 3.5% on April and continue with the erratic up-down performance seen so far this year, while building permits for May were up by 8.7% on April and were indeed the strongest seen since last December.  However, there are still fundamental issues with the housing sector which will not be ironed out for a considerable period of time.  As the building/construction sector tends to account for 40% of the total wire mill products market and takes a similar proportion of the overall tube and pipe produced for plumbing and heating tube, it is this sector which continues to act as the principal drag on copper’s recovery. 

**Improvement in copper consumption expected this year** We anticipate further gains in US copper demand this year, at reasonably rate 4-5%%.  This is much improved, though, on the 2-3% growth that we were expecting a quarter ago and the near 1% contraction in demand that we had pencilled in for 2011 in December of last year.  We now project that US and Canadian demand for copper will decline by 1.9% p.a. and 0.9% p.a., respectively out to 2025. 

The contraction reflects ongoing structural changes in the global economy which will see manufacturing and semis capacity relocating to lower wage economies.  Imports, rather than domestic production, will satisfy domestic copper demand.  Therefore, while the region’s wire and cable markets will be supported by the upgrading of much of its other infrastructure, this will not necessarily result in increased production of North American copper wire rod.  By 2025 we forecast that North American refined copper consumption will total ~1.45Mt.

This should not augur well for consumer confidence across the region and as such ought to be bad for economic activity also. However, every cloud has a silver lining and it would be churlish to dismiss the support that a weak currency provided in boosting exports and in doing so stimulating recovery in major industrial powerhouses like Germany in the aftermath of first stages of the ongoing debt crisis. **Western European outlook upgraded** Although the timing is a little unfortunate given the debt crises, we have actually upgraded our view on the economic outlook in Western Europe, compared to downgrades to other parts of the globe. Indeed, Eurozone industrial production continues to increase at a healthy rate, particularly on a year-on-year basis, with April’s data revealing a 6.1% expansion even if the rate of month-on-month growth has eased a little. For the year as a whole, we expect Eurozone IP to increase in the region of 5% in 2011 before easing to the 2-3% range for the following two years. Germany is leading this growth and we estimate growth in IP of just over 9% this year, following on from double-digit growth in 2010. **Wire rod leads European demand** Without doubt it is the wire rod market that is leading demand in Europe, with rod makers continuing to report healthy market conditions. Most rod producers expected demand strength to continue on from the strong end to 2010 and were set for continued growth but in most cases their expectations have been exceeded so far this year. Certainly, we expect some slowing in activity in the second half of the year but are still looking for a major part of overall demand growth coming from wire rod. In fact, it is strong output of Russian wire rod that is driving a sharp upturn in our forecast for Russian refined copper demand this year. We have discussed previously our expectations for this following the re-imposition of a tax on cathode exports and latest trade data confirms our view. Russian exports of wire rod are up by

over 130% at 116kt in the first four months of the year compared with the January-to-April period of 2010, while exports of refined copper have slumped by 61% to 65kt.  As a result of the increased domestic production of wire rod and as such, higher demand for cathode, we expect consumption growth of over 50% to 700kt this year, before growth eases back to more sensible growth rates in the low single-digit range thereafter.  Clearly this strong growth flatters our overall European demand estimate for this year. 

**Signs of substitution emerging elsewhere** While wire rod output drives overall demand higher, elsewhere some signs of slowing have emerged, with much of this easing being a result of the lofty copper price.  In short, high prices are resulting in substitution of copper in some application.  At this stage, it would appear that substitution is merely tempering the rate of growth in demand for copper products, rather than causing outright contraction but without doubt, this is an important development to keep abreast of.  Interestingly, the quarterly production results of a major European semis producer underline this. 

**Aurubis Q1 rod production outpaces shapes** Aurubis have released its latest quarterly production data, which revealed strong growth in wire rod output but a sharp slide in shapes.  Indeed, wire rod production rose by 11.3% year on year to 217kt and marking the second consecutive quarter-on-quarter increase.  However, output of shapes fell on a year-on-year and quarter-on-quarter basis, down by 17.9% to 46kt.  This is in line with our discussions with market participants who report strong demand for wire rod but that high copper prices are starting to temper growth in areas such us tubes and sheet and strip.  Output overall was higher by 4.8% year on year to 263kt and fits comfortably with our full year Western European refined demand forecast.

For the year as a whole, we expect European demand growth of just over 9%, which will actually be ahead of the pace of expansion in 2010.  However, as we noted above, this year’s increase is flattered somewhat by the 50% surge in Russian refined demand following tax changes there that have discouraged exports of cathode and indirectly encouraged exports of wire rod.  If all of the increase in Russian demand was stripped out of the European 2011 forecast then growth would be in the region of 3%, with Germany and Poland leading growth but Sweden and Spain relative laggards.  We expect demand will slow further in 2012 and 2013 and moreover, there will be a contraction in the later part of our forecast period as European first use demand for semis gradually loses out to emerging players.  In the period 2010 to 2025 the annual average growth rate will be 1.1%.

## Japan 

**Economic data underscore impact of disaster** Three months ago we discussed the likely impact of the earthquake and tsunami in Japan and we take no particular credit for revealing now that economic activity did indeed slow sharply. Japan slipped back into recession in the first quarter after GDP contracted by 0.9% quarter on quarter in the January-toMarch period, following on from decline in activity in the final quarter of last year.  Meanwhile, industrial output has been similarly buffeted, down by 2.0% on the fourth quarter of 2010.  However, given that the earthquake and tsunami struck in the mid part of March, it was always going to be the second quarter were the decline in activity was felt most acutely, and in fact, we estimate a slump in IP of a further 4.5% q-o-q in the April-to-June period.  The year-on-year comparisons could have looked a lot worse though, especially given the extremely lofty growth seen in the first half of last year, so an expected decline in IP of 7.5% y-o-y in Q2 isn’t that bad.  For the year as a whole, we expect IP to contract by around 2%. 

**Shipments hold up reasonably well…** Despite the sharp fall in economic and industrial activity, wire and cable and brass mill shipments have held up reasonably well, despite key sectors such as automotive and electronics grinding to a halt.  In fact, wire and cable shipments rose by 1.1% year on year in the first quarter and are still up by 0.5% year-to-date in the first four months of the year, despite sharp 6.5% and 1.4% year-on-year falls in March and April.  Brass mill shipments have fared worse, however, and fell by 1.4% in the first quarter and are down by 1.1% year-to-date.  Taken together, total shipments of wire and cable and brass mill products are down by 0.4% in the January-to-April period. 

**…supported by construction** As we noted above, shipments have performed better than might have been expected given the slump in industrial activity in March and April, but it was a boost to construction sector shipments that tempered the decline, with temporary housing for displaced people in the disaster struck region supporting activity.  However, much of this activity was expected to take place in April and May and as such, this

temporary benefit should be behind us. More worryingly, there is anecdotal evidence that firms stocked up in anticipation of the construction work but that the actual building of temporary housing was lower than expected. As such, this could point to shipments slipping back in June and thereafter. As yet the government hasn’t completed an overall plan for reconstruction, although it has approved a supplementary budget for this purpose. We therefore do not expect a significant boost to demand from the construction sector this year, with a modest upturn anticipated for 2012. Indeed, it is worth pointing out that if the level of temporary housing built of 52,000 units translates into the same number of houses that are re-built, this is still less than average housing starts per month in Japan of late. New scrap, or manufacturing scrap, is generated during the fabrication of copper products and returned to the mill for reprocessing, or sold, and is not considered a new source of copper supply. A manufacturer may generate up to 60% of scrap as clippings, trimmings, stampings, borings, and turnings when processing copper and copper-base products into finished articles. New scrap is termed "run-around" or home scrap (which does not enter the scrap statistics) when it is generated internally at the plant re-using it, or it may be called "purchased return scrap" when returned by a customer from a plant external to that purchasing and re-using it. Old scrap is generated from worn out, discarded or obsolete copper products and thus, is considered to be a “new” source of supply. ## Scrapping rates The availability of _old_ copper scrap is linked to

the volume of copper-containing products installed/purchased and their life cycles, or duration.  The life of copper in electrical equipment and machinery averages 30-35 years; in non-electrical machinery, 15 years; in housing, 35-75 years; in transportation, 10 years; in all other sectors, about 10 years.  The average for the industry is estimated to be 15-20 years.  The rate of (old) scrap recovery and its availability to be the market is limited not only by copper's long life, but also by the sensitivity of scrap collection rates to market prices. 

Over the past 20 years, the volume of _new_ copper scrap has not grown in line with industrial consumption of copper because manufacturing efficiencies have improved, leading to as much as a 50% fall in new scrap generation over the period. 

## Scrap usage 

Most old scrap recovered from the market place must be reprocessed either by smelting and refining, or, to a lesser extent, by leaching and electrowinning to form a pure copper product.  Fire refining in a reverberatory or other furnace may be sufficient for the better grades of scrap.  This latter process uses oxidation, fluxing and reduction, with a refined ingot, wire bar, slab, or billet usually being the end product. 

Certain products, such as brass rod (manufactured using 80-90% scrap) can contain higher amounts of scrap than others while still maintaining product quality tolerance.  Others, such as wire rod, must contain far less impurities (typically 5%) since these could affect the drawability (leading to snapping) of the wire rod in producing wire.  New scrap is readily used by brass and copper tube mills to generate new semi-fabricated forms with little additional treatment. Because minimal clean-up procedures are needed, this type of scrap is commonly called "direct melt", or No.1 scrap.  In general, No. 1 scrap is contained in copper and copper-alloy products, rather than wire rod.  Scrap purchases by brass mills are based primarily on activity levels at the mills and the relative price differential between cathode and No. 1 scrap, rather than the actual copper price.  When business conditions are strong, brass mills have access to large volumes of return scrap.  When manufacturing (and, possibly imports) decline, mills may be forced to increase their cathode purchases. 

Low copper prices over the period 1997-2003 led to a reduction in the availability of smelting and refining grade scrap with a corresponding decline in the processing of this material in countries such the USA and in Europe.  The notable exception has been China where there has been an upward trend in the treatment of smelting and refining grade scrap material.  Economic and environmental considerations have also played a major role, with the cost of environmental compliance often leading to plant closures, particularly in the USA.  This is despite the fact that the cost of recovering one tonne of copper from scrap is approximately half that of recovery through

the conventional route (concentratesmelting-refining). Secondary smelters and ingot markers typically consume the lion's share (90%) of No.2 scrap and most of the auto radiators and red brass scrap. ## Scrap consumption Copper produced from scrap (at smelters, refineries and in direct use) amounted to 4.62Mt in 2010, an increase of 8.6% on the prior year and accounting for 34% of copper consumed. Direct use scrap took the lions share, representing some 57% of copper produced from scrap, with smelters (25%) and refineries (18%) producing copper from the balance. Scrap use posted a strong recovery in 2010, after contraction in the previous two years as declining copper prices resulted in a lack of incentive to collect scrap while sluggish industrial production meant limited scrap generation. Between 1997 and 2003 there was a steady decline in overall scrap use, falling to a low of 28.5%, in 2003, before recovering to 34% in 2007. Having peaked in the early 1990s at around 8%, scrap consumed at smelters has stabilised in recent years at 6% of the total market, but since 2008 it has been above 7%. Barring the period 2002-2005 refining grade scrap use has been relatively stable over the past 18 years at 6% of total consumption. The largest variation has occurred in direct use, declining from 23% in the early 1990s to 18% in 2002 and 2003 but then recovering to 22% between 2004 and 2007 before falling back to 18% in 2010. **Our project incentive price over the period to 2025 is $2.50/lb** In terms of long-term cycle average prices, these are critically dependant upon the metal demand outlook and on capital and operating costs.  The incentive price methodology starts by estimating the demand for additional mine capacity after allowing for scrap usage and base case mine production changes. Based on our last update in 2010$, an incentive price of around $2.50/lb is reasonable over the period to 2025. The impact, post 2004 occurred from a low base and followed a prolonged period of depressed copper prices during which suppliers of equipment, consumables and services had been forced to drive down costs to remain competitive. Metals Market Service Long Term Outlook - June 2011 Page 30 of 33 Copper Long-term Outlook # Principle uses of copper Copper consumption can be divided into three main product groups which are copper wire rod, copper products and copper alloy products. Copper wire rod, which accounts for an estimated 55% of total Global consumption (i.e. including scrap) and ~70% of primary consumption, is copper’s main first use. With the exception of silver, copper has the highest electrical conductivity of all the metals. This helps to explain why the principal application for copper wire rod is wire and cable. Wire rod is consumed in five main wire and cable markets which include general and industrial cable, utility power cable, telecommunication cable, other insulated wire and winding wire. In general, wire and cable and copper products are consumed in five broad sectors: construction, electric and electronic products, industrial machinery and equipment, transportation equipment and consumer and general products. Of these, construction is the largest sector for consuming copper, accounting for 33% of total copper consumption. The main wire and cable and copper products consumed in the construction industry include building wire, power cable, copper plumbing and air conditioning tube, copper sheet and alloy products. Building wire is the largest of the wire and cable markets, accounting for ~35% of wire rod consumption. Rising intensity of use, in both the mature and developing economies, will be largely responsible for building wire maintaining this position. The number of electrical appliances used at home and at the workplace continues to rise, particularly in the mature economies, thereby leading to an increase in the number of power outlets needed per building. In addition, recent technical issues imply that more copper wire and cable will be needed in the future. One of these issues, electrical energy efficiency involves using less power to perform a given task by using more or heavier copper conductors. Finally, good power quality, defined as the uninterrupted, undistorted flow of electricity at the correct voltage, is also helping to drive up the demand for building wire due to higher power quality being achieved by installing additional circuits and heavier wires and cables. In contrast to the building and industrial

cable market, the power utility market is the smallest of all the wire and cable segments.  However, demand growth for power cable will be supported by both the general recovery in utility investment and the fact that copper, the mainstay of power grids worldwide, still has considerable potential to carry energy better and reduce losses than aluminium. 

Copper tube, which accounts for an estimated 13% of global refined copper consumption, is the largest of the copper product markets.  The two main uses are in plumbing and heating systems and in air conditioners and refrigeration (ACR tube).  The steady proliferation of plumbing amenities in and around the home, particularly as many houses built today within the mature economies have more than one bathroom, are largely responsible for copper plumbing tube demand growth.  Elsewhere, improved living standards in the developing economies, leading to higher demand for air conditioners, continues to boost demand for ACR tube.  This is particularly the case in China and India where improved power supply will lead to a surge in the consumption of air conditioners over the coming years.  Meanwhile in the mature economies, the market is being driven by external factors such as environmental issues, regulatory concerns and social demands for comfort. 

Other copper and copper alloy products consumed by the construction sector include copper sheet and strip, rods, bars and sections plus brass products.  Copper sheet is used for roofing, eaves gutters, drain pipes for rainwater and lining for facades, while rods bars and sections, along with brass products, are used for building fixture and fittings.  In hospitals, brass doorknobs and push plates are widely used because it has been proven that they help to reduce cross contamination. 

Electrical and electronic products are copper’s second largest consuming sector, accounting for 33% of total copper demand.  Copper containing electrical and electronic products include telecommunication cable, power cable, transformer windings, semiconductors and motors for heavy appliances. 

Since the early 1990s copper telecommunication cable has been largely substituted by fibre optic cable in long distance networks.  However, owing to its high cost, copper telecom cable has remained the preferred link between the main network and consumers.  In addition, the development of the internet and e-mail has further enhanced the role of copper in telecommunications in recent years.  The need for information to be carried quicker along the telecommunication network has led to the introduction of asymmetrical digital subscriber line technology (ADSL).  The ADSL is a dedicated circuit between a home and the telephone company’s central office that uses normal copper telephone lines.  The addition of an ADSL chip to the existing copper network means that users can download files around 15 times faster than an analogue dial-up connection. 

Dramatic gains in copper consumption to have

occurred within the home because of a system known to the telecommunications industry as ‘structured wiring’.  The cable carrying voice, computer and television signals is connected to a central hub in the home.  Individual cables then run independently from here to high-quality connections in rooms throughout the house.  Cables connected to the hub consist of four pairs of twisted wires, capable of carrying more electronic signals with less interference and resistance than the older four-stranded telephone wires. High-speed digital service lines now provide computer data transmission 50 to 270 times faster than that of the fastest dial-up modem connected to a telephone line.  More importantly, with the number of homes connected to the Internet and usage continuing to increase strongly, demand for higher quality copper telecommunication wire and cable is expected to surge in the coming years. 

The other main wire and cable segment to supply the electrical sector is winding wire.  Winding wire demand accounts for an estimated 20% of copper wire rod consumption, making it the third largest wire and cable market.  Applications include transformers, generators, stereos, television sets and motors.  Indeed, it is the need to improve electrical efficiency of this last application, particularly in the mature economies, that has generated the most growth in winding wire demand recently.  This is because improved electrical efficiency involves using a larger conductor in order to reduce electrical resistance, as well as ensuring that the proper voltages are delivered when needed.  In addition, the efficiency of electric motors is being improved further by introducing copper into the rotor as opposed to aluminium.  Meanwhile, in the developing economies, demand growth will mainly stem from increased consumption of electrical goods as disposable incomes rise. 

Copper’s third largest consuming sector, industrial machinery and equipment, accounts for 13% of total consumption. Both copper wire and cable and semi products supply this sector which includes equipment and machinery, industrial valves and fittings, off-highway vehicles and heat exchangers.  Copper wire and copper and copper alloy products are also used in transportation equipment, copper’s fourth largest category.  This includes the automotive, marine and aircraft/aerospace sectors.  It is within the automotive sec

tor that developments of new copper applications have been most concentrated in recent years. Prior to 1930 copper and brass, having excellent pressure containing and anticorrosion characteristics, were the favoured materials to be used in brake tubing. However, mass auto production in the 1940s led to the adoption of furnace-brazed steel tubing because it was much lower in cost. Although this form of tubing is still widely used today, copper has re-gained some of its lost market share through the introduction of a copper-nickel alloy (90% copper/10% nickel) which is more resistant to corrosion from road mud and salt than steel piping. Likewise, new technology has led to the development of a new brazed copper-brass automotive radiator which has the necessary requirements to recapture some of the market share displaced by aluminium over the past twenty years. Meanwhile, 42-volt systems, hybrid vehicles and numerous electrical and electronic applications provide additional growth prospects for the use of copper within the automotive sector Over the years the number of electrical and electronic components installed per unit has been rising steadily, thereby creating the need for growth in the power and signal distribution system (otherwise known as the wiring harness). Many of the electrical components will have to be redesigned in order to work effectively with the higher-voltage systems which could result in the copper content of some of the electrical components falling, but as more power becomes available, new electrical components will emerge. Such examples include electronic valve actuation and electric braking, resulting in several kilos of copper, per unit, being added. Forecasts have shown that over the next ten years, increases per vehicle will outweigh the decreases in copper required per component. Copper’s final end-use category is consumer and general products. Copper consumed in this sector accounts for 8% of total copper consumption. The three main end-uses are electrical appliances, military ordnance and coinage. The production of the new Euro coin in recent years has helped to support demand for copper and copper alloy products.
